content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the Flood (Noah's flood) primarily symbolizes God's judgment upon human sin combined with the salvation/preservation of a righteous remnant, and—via explicit New Testament typology—it prefigures Christian baptism, in which the believer passes through the waters of judgment into cleansing and new life.","primary_basis":["Genesis 6:5-8; 6:11-13; 7:17-24 (judgment on universal wickedness)","Genesis 6:8-9; 7:1; 8:15-9:17 (preservation of Noah, covenant, new creation/new beginning)","1 Peter 3:18-22 (the flood waters as a type/antitype of baptism)","2 Peter 2:5 and 2 Peter 3:5-7 (flood as paradigm of divine judgment, parallel to final judgment by fire)","Matthew 24:37-39 / Luke 17:26-27 ('as in the days of Noah'—flood as figure of sudden eschatological judgment)","Hebrews 11:7 (Noah's ark and salvation by faith)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Eschatological warning: the flood as a type of the sudden, unexpected final judgment at Christ's return ('as in the days of Noah').","basis":["Matthew 24:37-39","Luke 17:26-27","2 Peter 3:5-7"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Baptismal typology emphasized as the primary sense (especially in patristic, Catholic, Orthodox, and liturgical traditions, where the flood appears in baptismal liturgies and catechesis).","basis":["1 Peter 3:20-21","Patristic usage (e.g., Tertullian, On Baptism; Augustine; Catechism of the Catholic Church §1219)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"De-creation and re-creation: the flood as a reversal of Genesis 1 (return of chaos waters) followed by a new creation and renewed covenant/mandate—a prominent reading in academic biblical theology.","basis":["Genesis 1:2 compared with Genesis 7:11 (fountains of the deep, windows of heaven)","Genesis 8:1 (wind/Spirit over the waters echoing Gen 1:2)","Genesis 9:1-7 (renewed creation mandate)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Flood/deep waters more broadly as a symbol of overwhelming trouble, distress, death, or chaotic evil from which God delivers—apart from the Noah narrative.","basis":["Psalm 69:1-2, 14-15","Psalm 32:6","Psalm 18:4, 16","Isaiah 43:2","Jonah 2:3-5"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The ark (rather than the flood itself) as a type of Christ or of the Church, with the flood as the judgment one is saved through only by being 'in' the ark—classic patristic and Reformed typology.","basis":["Genesis 6-8","1 Peter 3:20-21","Augustine, City of God 15; Cyprian's 'no salvation outside the church' imagery"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The flood as an image of satanic or persecuting opposition against God's people (a 'flood from the dragon's mouth').","basis":["Revelation 12:15-16","Isaiah 59:19 (in some translations: 'when the enemy comes in like a flood')"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Flood imagery as an outpouring of blessing or of the Spirit (positive flood imagery), occasionally invoked in devotional and charismatic usage.","basis":["Isaiah 44:3","Amos 5:24 (justice rolling like waters)","Malachi 3:10 (overflowing blessing)"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a recognizable, broadly settled consensus: the flood symbolizes divine judgment on sin paired with the salvation of a faithful remnant, and the New Testament itself fixes two interpretive lines—baptismal typology (1 Peter 3) and eschatological warning (Matthew 24 / 2 Peter 3). The alternatives listed are largely complementary emphases rather than competing meanings; which one is foregrounded varies by tradition (liturgical traditions stress baptism; evangelical preaching stresses judgment and the days-of-Noah warning; academic biblical theology stresses de-creation/re-creation). This assessment is made blind to the author's material, as instructed."}
